P1.label: Strong pattern
P1.constraint: Decision authority is more centralized than the business requires
P1.diagnosis: Accountability has been assigned without matching authority. So people check before acting, decisions queue upward, and speed drops. Leaders see the hesitancy and hold tighter, which shrinks the authority further. The loop is stable and it is getting worse.
supports: High: Leadership prefers to decide centrally
High: People lack the authority they're accountable for
High: Managers' decisions get reversed
High: Decisions escalate to the top
High: People don't feel authorized to decide
High: Decisions wait on a person
High: People lack the authority to act
Medium: People wait for direction before deciding
Medium: Decisions drift upward when things feel risky
Low: Control is added after problems

open.question: When it doesn't happen, what usually gets in the way?

forces.t: Decisions drift upward whenever things feel risky.
Control is added in response to problems, and each layer slows the next decision.
Authority was never written down, so it defaults to whoever is most senior.

P1.blind: The organization may have normalised escalation as diligence.

notDo.t: Don't fix this with an empowerment programme.
notDo.d: People don't need to be told they are empowered. They need one decision they are allowed to make, in writing, and a leader who doesn't overrule it.

experiment.hypothesis: Decision authority is too concentrated at the top.
steps: Identify the five recurring decisions consuming the most senior-leadership time.
Move two of them down one level for 30 days, with written guardrails and a named owner.
Tell the people who used to make them that they no longer do.
watch: Decision cycle time
Number of escalations
Leadership hours recovered

P2.label: High confidence
P2.constraint: Too many priorities, and no clear sense of what to stop
P2.diagnosis: Priorities accumulate and nothing is formally retired. Capacity is spread across more work than exists to do it, so everything moves slowly and the urgent displaces the important. The missing decision is not what to start. It is what to stop.
supports: High: Priorities exceed capacity
High: Commitments compete for the same capacity
High: Nothing is formally stopped
Medium: It's unclear what could be stopped
Medium: Capacity is committed past what exists
Medium: New priorities are added faster than old ones are retired
Low: Agreed priorities sometimes slip
Low: People aren't sure what matters most

forces.t: New priorities are added faster than old ones are retired.
The difficult conversation is being avoided, so the cause stays unnamed.
Stopping something feels like failure, so nothing is formally stopped.

P2.blind: Your organization may have normalised overload as a sign of ambition.

notDo.d: Scoring forty initiatives produces a ranked list of forty initiatives. The missing decision is what to stop, and frameworks are how organizations avoid making it.

experiment.hypothesis: The organization has committed to more than it can deliver and stops nothing.
steps: List every active priority, everywhere.
Rank by contribution to the one thing that matters most. Stop the bottom fifth explicitly.
Watch for a month what actually gets worse.
watch: Share of capacity on the top three priorities
Agreed work delivered on time
Things that got worse after stopping

P3.label: High confidence
P3.constraint: Performance depends on people working around the system
P3.diagnosis: The system doesn't carry the work, so capable people carry it personally. Results still arrive, which is why the gap is invisible, and the heroics get rewarded, which is why it persists. This works at the current size and breaks at the next one.
supports: High: Performance depends almost entirely on heroics
High: Problems recur
High: Repeatability depends on the person
Medium: Recurrences are solved as new events
Low: Best people are often on urgent, low-value work

forces.t: Each recurrence is solved as a new event rather than traced to its cause.
Nothing about the current pattern requires anyone to act, so it persists.
The people who make it happen are the most valued, so the workaround is the career path.

P3.blind: Your team may have learned to work around the system rather than improve it.

notDo.t: Don't fix this by hiring more of the people who make it happen.
notDo.d: Heroics that work at this size won't at the next. You would be scaling the workaround, and paying for it twice.

experiment.hypothesis: The system doesn't carry the work, so people carry it by hand.
steps: Ask your three most relied-upon people what they do by hand that the process should do.
Pick the one that consumes the most time.
Design it into the process, remove the manual step, and credit them for surfacing it.
watch: Hours per week on recurring workarounds
Recurrences of the problem
Results when the key person is away

P4.label: Emerging pattern
P4.constraint: Leadership isn't aligned on what matters most
P4.diagnosis: Your leadership team appears to hold different versions of what the business must accomplish. Each version is defensible, which is why it persists. The organization below is executing several strategies at once and experiencing it as slowness.
supports: High: Leaders hold very different priorities
High: Leadership holds different priorities
High: Decisions wait on leadership agreement
High: Leadership disagreement stalls decisions
Medium: Analysis starts a debate about what it means

open.question: What most limits people's ability to act?

forces.t: The difficult conversation is being avoided, so the cause stays unnamed.
New priorities are added faster than old ones are retired.
Priorities are set function by function rather than for the business as a whole.

P4.blind: Your leadership team may have learned to treat polite agreement as alignment.

notDo.t: Don't fix this with a communication plan.
notDo.d: The problem isn't that the strategy hasn't been communicated. It's that it hasn't been chosen. Communicating three versions more clearly produces three clearer versions.

experiment.hypothesis: Leadership holds different versions of what matters most.
steps: Ask each leader to write, alone, the three things the business must accomplish this year.
Compare the lists in one room. Do not leave until it is one list.
Publish it and retire what didn't survive.
watch: Distinct top priorities named across leadership
Decisions reopened after being made
Conflicting requests reaching teams

P5.label: Emerging pattern
P5.constraint: It isn't safe to raise problems or disagree
P5.diagnosis: Raising a problem carries risk, so problems surface late and decisions rest on filtered information. Bad decisions persist longer than they should, trust in leadership erodes, and even less gets said. This is the friction that hides all the others.
supports: High: The last person to raise a problem paid for it
High: Problems aren't raised openly
High: Mistakes are costly, so people don't act
High: Raising problems is difficult
Medium: The difficult conversation is avoided
Low: Managers check before deciding

forces.t: The difficult conversation is being avoided, so the cause stays unnamed.
Current incentives reward the behaviour that produces the friction.
The last person who raised a hard truth paid for it, and everyone remembers.

P5.blind: The organization may have learned that silence is loyalty.

notDo.t: Don't fix this with an anonymous survey or a values poster.
notDo.d: Safety is created in the moment a leader responds to bad news, and destroyed the same way. Everything else is theatre.

experiment.hypothesis: Raising problems carries a cost, so problems surface late.
steps: Open your main leadership meeting with "what's not working?" before any status. The most senior person speaks last.
Thank the first person who names a real problem, publicly, and act on it within the week.
Repeat weekly for a quarter.
watch: Problems raised before they become incidents
Time from problem noticed to problem raised
Disagreements voiced in the meeting

P6.label: Emerging pattern

P6.diagnosis: Your most capable people have become the default fix for everything. Their time fills with urgent, low-leverage work, and the highest-value problems get whoever is free. Results plateau, the best people are stretched thinner, and eventually they leave or disengage.

High: Top people spend their time on rescue work

Low: Performance depends on workarounds

open.question: When it doesn't happen, what usually gets in the way?

forces.t: Each recurrence is solved as a new event rather than traced to its cause.
Current incentives reward the behaviour that produces the friction.
Whoever is most capable gets pulled into every fire, because it works.

P6.blind: Your organization may have normalised using its best people as the emergency service.

notDo.t: Don't fix this by hiring more senior people.
notDo.d: You are not short of talent. You are spending the talent you have on the wrong problems, and new talent would be spent the same way.

experiment.hypothesis: Your best people are being spent on urgent work instead of the highest-value problems.
steps: For your five most capable people, list where their time went last week.
Move each one's largest block of low-value work to someone else, or stop it.
Put the freed time on the one problem that matters most and protect it for a quarter.
watch: Top talent time on the top three priorities
Fires handled by someone other than the best people
Progress on the protected problem
